newsitem.title: USA: Baby talk subject of White House conference.
newsitem.headline: Baby talk subject of White House conference.

text.p: President Clinton and Hillary Rodham Clinton Thursday staged a celebration of the virtues of baby talk.

It was the White House Conference on Early Child Development and Learning, which brought together some of America's top experts to urge parents to devote time and attention to children's learning at the earliest possible age -- even if their babbling makes no sense to the untrained ear.

"Fifteen years ago we thought that a baby's brain structure was virtually complete at birth," Mrs. Clinton said. "Now we understand that it is a work in progress and that everything we do with a child has some kind of potential physical influence on that rapidly forming brain."

Experts told the East Room gathering, beamed by satellite to 92 other sites around the country, that babies learn the sounds of language in their early months and need to be talked to and sung to frequently in their first three years.

"When we speak to our children something is happening," said Dr. Patricia Kuhl, head of the speech and hearing sciences department at the University of Washington in Seattle. "We are bringing about changes in the brain that will allow them to participate in the communication game. Infants are born to learn. Our role is to be good partners in this learning process."

The conference was the work of Mrs. Clinton, long a children's advocate and author of a best-selling book about child-rearing, "It Takes a Village." President Clinton noted that at the time he met his future wife she was working at Yale University's Child Study Centre.

"Being a parent is a joy and a challenge," said the president, who with his wife is the parent of a daughter, Chelsea, 17. "But it's not a job you can walk away from, take a vacation from, or even apply for family leave from."

Mrs. Clinton said she wanted to stress that activities that are "the easiest, cheapest and most fun to do with your child are also the best for his or her development -- singing, playing games, reading, story-telling, just talking and listening."

To illustrate the unformed nature of the early brain, Dr. Carla Shatz of the University of California at Berkeley said adults with cataracts may see fine after surgery but babies born with them will grow up blind. "The eye that wasn't used because it had the cataract actually lost many of its connections with the brain. They withered away," she said. "This is a classic example of 'use it, or lose it.'"
Dr. Terry Brazelton of Harvard Medical School urged the Clintons to pursue universal health care, at least for children.

Clinton said he proposed in his fiscal 1988 budget to extend health care coverage to as many as 5 million uncovered children by 2000. He said he also wanted to work harder to protect children living in fear of abuse and violence.
"It is appalling the number of letters I get from 5- and 6-year-olds who simply want me to make their lives safe," he said.
